# Concepts and pitfalls {#sec-pitfalls}

```{r}
source("R/book.R")
ps <- read_pipeline("outputs", "quality", "pca_status_by_year.csv")
dy <- read_pipeline("outputs", "quality", "dft_stock_by_year.csv")
```

This chapter collects, in one place, the things most likely to lead an
analysis astray. Each is explained in more detail elsewhere in the book.

## 1. Observed is not the same as the fleet

A vehicle is *observed* in a year when it has a postcode area in that year.
That does not mean it was tested that year: the postcode area is copied back
from a vehicle's first MOT to its first registration, and carried forward for
about two years after its last (@sec-lifecycle). The observed vehicles are not
the whole fleet: SORN vehicles, most heavy vehicles, most vehicles over 40 and,
in the last three years, new vehicles not yet tested are missing
(@sec-mot-test). For cars aged three to
about sixteen, the observed count is close to DfT's count of registered
vehicles (@sec-data-quality).

**What to do:** say "vehicles observed" or "vehicles tested", not "vehicles
registered" or "the fleet", and compare with DfT's figures for ages three and
over.

## 2. The last three years are incomplete

```{r}
peak <- ps$year[which.max(ps$pca)]
cars <- subset(dy, body_type == "Cars")
```

The number of vehicles observed peaks in `r peak` and then falls
(@fig-pca-status). This is not a shrinking fleet. A new car has no location
until its first MOT at three years old, so cars first registered in 2023 to
2025 are almost entirely missing, and the final year, 2025, is also only
partly covered. In 2025 the CARS count of cars of all ages is
`r round(cars$ratio_mot_to_dft[cars$year == 2025], 2)` of DfT's, against
`r round(cars$ratio_mot_to_dft[cars$year == 2018], 2)` in 2018.

**What to do:** for trends in the whole fleet, stop three years before the end
of the data, or restrict to vehicles aged three and over. Never read a trend
into the final year. Be especially careful with anything that is growing
fast among new vehicles, such as electric cars, whose share is understated in
recent years.

## 3. Location is where the vehicle was tested

The postcode area is that of the MOT testing station (@sec-geography).

**What to do:** describe results as "vehicles tested in" an area. Do not
treat a change of area as a change of address without saying so.

## 4. Dead is not scrapped, and unknown is not missing at random

`dead` means "not tested since", which includes vehicles scrapped, exported,
on SORN or exempt. `unknown` covers new vehicles not yet tested and long
gaps in a vehicle's history (@sec-lifecycle). Because a postcode area is
carried forward for about two years after the last MOT, a vehicle only
becomes `dead` some time after it stopped being tested.

**What to do:** call a vehicle that has become `dead` one that "stopped being
tested", not "scrapped", unless you have other evidence. Remember that vehicles
last seen in the final two years have not yet had the chance to become
`dead`.

## 5. Averages depend on who is in the denominator

Average mileage is calculated over the vehicles with a (plausible) mileage
that year, a group that changes from year to year and differs from the
vehicles counted. Averages of averages are wrong (@sec-aggregate-tables).

**What to do:** compute averages as total ÷ count over exactly the group you
mean, and report the count alongside.

## 6. Mileage needs a test at each end

Annual mileage is shared out from the distance between two tests
(@sec-sources-linkage). A year after a vehicle's last test has no mileage; a
long gap between tests spreads its distance across the gap, hiding any
variation within it. 2020 is particularly affected by delayed tests.

**What to do:** compare years with similar coverage; be careful with
year-on-year changes around 2020, and with vehicles near the start or end of
their lives.

## 7. Recorded, filled and assumed values

Many harmonised values were filled from similar vehicles or assumed from rules
(@sec-pipeline). Most Euro statuses are assumed from dates; CO~2~, weight and
type approval are often filled from similar vehicles.

**What to do:** check the `_src` column, and repeat key results using recorded
values only. If the result changes, report both.

## 8. Plug-in hybrids are a lower bound

Plug-in hybrids are identified from DfT's records by model, and models sold
both ways are left as ordinary hybrids (@sec-fuels-emissions).

**What to do:** report plug-in hybrid numbers as "at least", or combine all
hybrids.

## 9. Classifications differ between sources

MOT class 4 is not the same as DfT's cars (@sec-vehicle-types).

**What to do:** use `body_type` when comparing with DfT, and state which
classification you used.

## 10. Postcode areas are big

Postcode areas average over very different places, and patterns between
areas may not hold within them (@sec-geography).

**What to do:** use postcode area results for broad comparisons, not to
describe neighbourhoods or individuals.

## 11. Northern Ireland is different

Northern Ireland tests at four years in government test centres, its test
class is not supplied, and its testing was disrupted in 2020. It is coded
`NI`, a single area.

**What to do:** consider analysing Great Britain on its own, as the fleet
profile tables do.

## 12. Identifiers change between versions

`vehicle_id` is not stable between versions of the data (@sec-data-products).

**What to do:** join on `registration_DVSA`, and record which version of the
data you used.
